clue.text: Welshman's platform

parts.note: Dai is the stock Welsh man's name in crosswords, short for David, and the possessive adds an S
Dai is the stock Welsh man's name in crosswords, short for David, and the possessive adds an S

explanation.surface: A Welshman shows off the stage he owns.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais is a raised stage at one end of a hall, a kind of low platform.

clue.text: Mary's woven Luke's odd skullcap

indicators.note: woven says the letters of the first name are twisted together into a new order

parts.note: the name Mary, its possessive giving no letter

indicators.note: odd says the letters of the second name come out strangely ordered

parts.note: the name Luke, its possessive giving no letter

explanation.surface: Mary has knitted Luke a peculiar little cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woven' turns MARY into YARM and 'odd' turns LUKE into ULKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarmulke is the small round cap worn by Jewish men, a skullcap by another name.

clue.text: Can university upset one?

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the whole run of letters upside down, so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A question of whether a university could overturn something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns TINU into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single thing, one whole counted on its own.

clue.text: It's not fair for all to see kinky singles

parts.note: U is the British film certificate for a universal audience, suitable for everyone

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of the word singles are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that kinky single people are flaunting themselves publicly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kinky' turns SINGLES into GLINESS. Fair here means beautiful, so what is not fair is plainness; the U is the British film rating for all audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in its old sense means lovely to look at, and its opposite quality is a lack of good looks.

clue.text: A lot of geese going outside in a strong wind

indicators.note: in says the outer letters of going sit within the word for a strong wind

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

indicators.note: outside picks only the outer letters of the word going

explanation.surface: Geese flying on through a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going outside' reads as a phrase about the geese heading out, but 'outside' only picks the ends of 'going'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaggle is the collective noun for a flock of geese on the ground.

clue.text: Amazed, astounded, startled at first with weight one lost

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: a ton is a unit of weight
I is the Roman numeral for one
shed means got rid of, lost

explanation.surface: A dieter is amazed and startled at having lost a stone or so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' takes AS from 'astounded' and 'startled'. 'astounded' and 'startled' read like more synonyms for the definition but only give their first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonished is a direct synonym of amazed, both meaning greatly surprised.

clue.text: Fashion to vary for dedicated follower

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters of the next two words are worked into a new form

explanation.surface: A dedicated follower of fashion likes to vary things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' turns TO VARY into the answer; the surface recalls the Kinks song Dedicated Follower of Fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A votary is a devoted adherent of a religion or cause, someone dedicated to it.

clue.text: One Roman not entirely a well respected man

indicators.note: not entirely says the letters are taken from inside the phrase without using all of it

explanation.surface: A Roman citizen who is not quite a man of good standing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is ironic: this emperor was anything but respected, echoing the irony of the Kinks song A Well Respected Man.
explanation.definitionFit: The emperor is called a well respected man sarcastically, since he was notorious for cruelty.

clue.text: Election success for party once more?

definitions.meaning: a seat won from a rival is a gain for the party, read as two words

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is a gain at the polls; as one word it means a second time.

clue.text: Old politician pleased to receive a few pounds

indicators.note: to receive says the first word is followed by and takes on the weight that comes next

parts.note: glad means pleased
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A former MP is delighted to be paid some money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a few pounds' suggests money but is the stone, a British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: William Gladstone was a Victorian Liberal Prime Minister, an old politician.

clue.text: It's not this that's exceptional

definitions.meaning: literally an alternative thing, not the one in front of you
the slang phrase means remarkable, out of the ordinary

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally means a different thing and colloquially means quite remarkable.

clue.text: Protagonists content here in New Zealand

indicators.note: content means what something holds, so the answer lies inside the word

explanation.surface: The leading characters are happy living in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like an adjective meaning happy; it is the noun, what the word holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago is a region in the south of New Zealand's South Island.

clue.text: Large glen I've turned over as land for the community

indicators.note: turned over says the letters of the three words are churned into another order, like soil

explanation.surface: A big valley has been ploughed to become common ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' rearranges LARGEGLENIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A village green is a common open space owned by a village and used by all its residents.

clue.text: Blurred vision commencing with fever

indicators.note: commencing takes just the start of the word vision

parts.note: ague is an old word for a fever with shivering

explanation.surface: A patient's eyesight blurs as a fever starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Vague means indistinct or unclear in outline, like a blurred image.

clue.text: New moon Indian used to denote age

indicators.note: new says the letters of the next two words are made afresh in another order

explanation.surface: An Indian lunar calendar used to date things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges MOONINDIAN. 'New moon' looks like a single phrase, but 'New' only signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, abbreviated AD, labels years of the Christian era.

clue.text: Furies in ancient Greece and Ireland? Certainly!

parts.note: Erin is a poetic name for Ireland
yes is an emphatic certainly

explanation.surface: Someone checks that there were Furies in both Greece and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Erinyes were the Greek goddesses of vengeance, called the Furies by the Romans.

clue.text: Plant for southern border

parts.note: an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A gardener picks something to plant along a southern border.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedge is a grass-like plant of wet ground.

clue.text: See 13
Instant wine designation

definitions.meaning: on a wine label the French word means dry

explanation.definitionFit: Sec is short for second, a moment, and the French label for dry wine.

clue.text: Secure accommodation is sheltering street musicians

parts.note: a cell is a locked room in a prison

indicators.note: sheltering says the word is wraps round the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A hostel takes in buskers playing on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'street musicians' reads as one phrase, but 'street' gives ST and 'musicians' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellists are musicians who play the cello.

clue.text: What a feller did — he got married

parts.note: taken as written
wed means got married

explanation.surface: Asked what the chap did, the answer is that he married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feller' looks like slang for fellow, a man; here it is one who fells trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodcutter cuts down trees with an axe, so what he did was chop.

clue.text: Historic engagement in station

definitions.meaning: the 1815 battle where Napoleon was defeated

explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo was the 1815 battle and is a big London railway station named after it.

clue.text: See a change — Unionists became less severe

indicators.note: change says the letters of see and a are swapped round into another order

parts.note: the DUP is Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party

explanation.surface: Politicians in Northern Ireland soften their stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' turns SEEA into EASE. The DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease up is a phrasal verb meaning to relax or become less harsh.

clue.text: Fat Poles dropping in at the end of the day

indicators.note: dropping in says the poles are dropped inside the word for fat

parts.note: suet is hard animal fat
N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Overweight Polish visitors call round in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; it is the two magnetic poles, N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunset is the time the sun goes down, closing the day.

clue.text: Two hands needed for fruit

indicators.note: two calls for the next word twice over

parts.note: paw is informal for hand

explanation.surface: Peeling this fruit takes both hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Pawpaw is another name for the papaya, a tropical fruit.

clue.text: Binge drinker, perhaps, extremely demonstrative, taking drink outside

indicators.note: taking drink outside says the coffee goes round the selected letters

parts.note: a latte is a milky coffee drink

indicators.note: extremely picks the first and last letters of demonstrative

explanation.surface: An extrovert who drinks to excess goes out for another.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladette is a British term for a young woman who drinks heavily and behaves rowdily like a lad; 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladette is a young woman who behaves in a boisterous way, often binge drinking, so a binge drinker is an example.

clue.text: Note car on motorway

parts.note: the Mini is a small British car
M is the British abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A memo about a car on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests a written memo; it is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A minim is a musical note worth half a semibreve, a half note.

clue.text: American form (non-U) in Flintshire town

indicators.note: non-U, read literally, says the letter U is taken out

parts.note: a mould is a form for shaping

explanation.surface: A Welsh town uses an American spelling, not posh enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' says the result is the US spelling of the word. Non-U is British slang for not upper-class; Mold is a town in Flintshire, north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Mold is the county town of Flintshire in north Wales.

clue.text: Water girl is swimming — that's very obvious

indicators.note: is swimming says the letters of the two words move around freely into a new order

explanation.surface: Plain to see that a girl is swimming in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is swimming' rearranges WATERGIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: Writ large means made prominent or clearly evident, so very obvious.

clue.text: Laughing out loud with a girl from Copacabana

parts.note: LOL is texting shorthand for laughing out loud

explanation.surface: A joke shared with a girl in a Rio nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: Copacabana is Barry Manilow's song whose showgirl is named Lola.
explanation.definitionFit: Lola is the showgirl heroine of the song Copacabana.

clue.text: See 11
Get up late and hesitate to prepare an ambush

parts.note: to lie in is to stay in bed late
to wait is to hold back, hesitate

explanation.surface: Someone oversleeps and dawdles before setting a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is to hide ready to attack, setting an ambush.

clue.text: Weaving machinery appears ominously close

definitions.meaning: frames on which cloth is woven
to rise up threateningly near at hand

explanation.definitionFit: Looms are weaving frames, and to loom is to tower up menacingly.
